qualification: Static future GNU 5.3 questions, not tests or observed tuples. Every PROJECTcandidate is a source-grounded proposal, not ratified. Native output cannot authorize product work.

rows.question: Does an already-exported scalar convert to indexed, and how do native declaration/export listings represent it?
rows.script:

a=([2]=two)
printf 'assignment=%s\n' "$?"
declare -p a
export -p
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Reject indexed conversion of exported scalar before RHS, status 1; preserve scalar and export membership. Deliberately stricter than any unobserved native behavior.
rows.qualification: Native declaration/export listing only; not external-process environment proof.

rows.question: What does native export of an existing array do, including empty elements and attribute display?
rows.script:

printf 'export=%s\n' "$?"

rows.PROJECTcandidate: Reject export a with status 1, preserve unexported indexed binding; do not serialize zero or JSON. Product export-p remains unsupported.

rows.question: How do declare +a and whole-variable unset differ for conversion back to scalar?
rows.script:

declare +a a
printf 'plus_a=%s\n' "$?"
declare -p a
unset a
a=scalar
declare -p a

rows.qualification: Native declaration attribute behavior remains unknown until GO.

rows.question: How are a readonly empty array and failed unset displayed?
rows.script:
a=()
readonly a
declare -p a
readonly -p
unset a

declare -p a

rows.qualification: GNU may list unrelated startup readonly names; retain bounded exact output without assuming a line count.

rows.question: Does local a retain indexed kind without values, and does local a=value restore outer sparse contents on return?
rows.script:
a=([2]=outer [7]='')
f() { local a; declare -p a; local a=inner; declare -p a; return 7; }
f
printf 'function=%s\n' "$?"
declare -p a

rows.question: Does unsetting local array expose outer immediately, and what kind is a subsequent local assignment?
rows.script:
a=([2]=outer)
f() { local a=inner; unset a; declare -p a; a=scalar; declare -p a; }
f
declare -p a

rows.question: Can local shadow readonly outer indexed binding with or without initializer?
rows.script:

f() { local a; printf 'local=%s\n' "$?"; local a=inner; printf 'initialized=%s\n' "$?"; declare -p a; }

rows.qualification: Keeps accepted scalar readonly-shadow rule; no claimed GNU diagnostic parity.

rows.question: Which export/readonly attributes survive local creation, local unset and return?
rows.script:
export a=outer
f() { local a; declare -p a; unset a; a=inner; readonly a; declare -p a; return 4; }
f
printf 'function=%s\n' "$?"
declare -p a
export -p
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Scalar local creation preserves accepted export membership; unset removes it; local readonly changes are removed on return and whole exported outer restored. Indexed local snapshots follow the same full-attribute discipline.
rows.qualification: Focused scalar-attribute boundary companion, not a new scalar implementation or passing array case.

rows.question: During compound replacement, do RHS references see old elements or earlier entries of the replacement?
rows.PROJECTcandidate: All RHS references resolve live prior target, never private stage; replacement publication is one guarded transfer.
rows.qualification: RHS visibility is an open native qualification, not assumed from documentation.

rows.question: During compound append with an explicit replacement index, do later RHS references see earlier staged replacement?
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Clone old slots, stage changes, RHS sees prior target; no intermediate target publication.

rows.question: Does known readonly compound target prevent RHS state effects, and what state is visible on shell exit?
rows.script:
a=([0]=old)
side=before
readonly a
trap 'declare -p a side fresh' EXIT
a=("${side:=kept}" "${fresh:=created}")
printf 'assignment=%s fresh=%s\n' "$?" "${fresh-unset}"
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Known readonly array fails before array RHS, no fresh assignment; existing scalar RHS-before-readonly path is unchanged.
rows.qualification: Static EXIT trap inspects target/side/fresh even if native terminates, retaining a missing-name diagnostic when applicable. No assumed exit status.

rows.question: After a later RHS parameter error, are earlier target entries published and are unrelated RHS assignments retained?
rows.script:
a=([0]=old [5]=tail)
trap 'declare -p a side' EXIT
a=([0]=new [1]="${side:=kept}" [2]="${missing:?preseal-stop}")
printf 'after\n'
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Discard target stage; preserve side=kept and original target unless RHS independently mutated it. Expansion failure remains primary.
rows.qualification: EXIT trap is fixed builtin inspection; parameter-error termination is not set-e behavior.

rows.question: What happens when a RHS scalar-default assignment mutates the same array whose zero element was absent?
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Parameter assignment writes zero once on live target and advances version; stage rejects stale target status 1, preserving RHS mutation and old element 2 without resurrection/retry.
rows.qualification: Parent-state self-mutation via parameter assignment, not arithmetic or a subshell-reentrancy claim.

rows.question: Does readonly set by a function in command substitution affect parent target attributes?
rows.script:
a=([0]=old)
f() { readonly a; printf replacement; }
a=("$(f)")
declare -p a
rows.PROJECTcandidate: Function runs in isolated substitution clone, so readonly is not a parent race; RHS executes once and parent staged replacement can publish absent other conflicts.
rows.qualification: Cannot qualify host/async parent readonly timing or cancellation. Exactly one command-substitution child context.

rows.question: Does an owned-file RHS effect survive a later compound expansion failure while target state is inspectable?
rows.script:
a=([0]=old)
f() { printf 'kept\n' > "$TMPDIR/rhs.txt"; printf replacement; }
trap 'declare -p a; IFS= read -r receipt < "$TMPDIR/rhs.txt"; printf "receipt=%s\n" "$receipt"' EXIT
a=("$(f)" "${missing:?preseal-stop}")

rows.qualification: Only future fixture write, five fixed bytes, one substitution child; no file or native process created during preseal.
